title: Universal energy barrier for plastic flow in a network glass
authors: Ibrahim Ghanem, Richard Jana, Wolfram G. Nöhring, Michael Moseler, Lars Pastewka
abstract: Shear transformations are the elementary events of plasticity in glasses and underpin many mesoscopic models of plastic flow, yet their atomic origin and energetics remain difficult to establish. Here we use a machine-learned interatomic potential to show that, in amorphous carbon as a representative network glass, a shear transformation corresponds to the breaking or formation of a single covalent bond. The simplicity of the associated reaction coordinate, the bond length, enables us to extract energy landscapes and barriers. Despite the intrinsic structural disorder, we find that all energy landscapes collapse onto a universal barrier shape. What remains bond-specific is a single scale, the bond-jump distance, which fixes the barrier height through a cubic law. Combined with the activation statistics of shear transformations, this yields a model that predicts the plastic flow stress from independently determined bond-level quantities. Our results provide microscopic support for phenomenological models of plastic flow in glasses and suggest a route towards a quantitative description of amorphous plasticity.
summary: This work provides a microscopic theory for plastic flow in amorphous glasses by showing that plasticity is mediated by single covalent bond breaking/forming events. By analyzing the energy barriers of these events, the authors demonstrate that the energy landscape is universal, allowing them to predict the macroscopic plastic flow stress from simple, bond-level parameters.
main_problem: The paper aims to establish the atomic origin and energetics of shear transformations (STs), the fundamental events governing plasticity in amorphous glasses, and link these microscopic rules to macroscopic flow stress.
main_result: The energy landscapes associated with STs collapse onto a universal shape, and the plastic flow stress can be quantitatively predicted from bond-level quantities using a cubic scaling law.
method: The authors used machine-learned interatomic potentials to simulate shear deformation in amorphous carbon, analyzing the energy barriers of single-bond breaking/forming events.
model_or_system: The system studied is amorphous carbon (a-C), modeled as a network glass. The analysis focuses on the energy landscape of a single covalent bond, which is assumed to govern the elementary plastic event.
key_observables: Plastic flow stress ($\sigma_F$), energy barrier ($E_b$), bond-jump distance ($\Delta\ell$), and the Gini coefficient ($G$) for shear localization.
important_parameters: Bond-jump distance ($\Delta\ell_0$), density ($ho$), and the coordination number ($\langle z angle$).
main_assumptions: Plasticity is governed solely by the breaking or formation of single covalent bonds, and the energy landscape of these events is universal and independent of local structure.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the stress-strain response showing stress drops (STs), the collapse of energy landscapes onto a universal curve, and the cubic scaling of the intrinsic barrier with the bond-jump distance.
paper_structure: The work progresses from identifying STs in the macroscopic stress-strain response to analyzing the universal energy barrier shape, deriving scaling laws for the barrier height, and finally constructing a model that predicts the flow stress from these microscopic bond-level parameters.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter plasticity, the use of machine-learned potentials and the concept of universal energy barriers in disordered systems connect to the study of complex energy landscapes found in quantum many-body systems.
